_insn_remainder: The four cases of 9173 that do not match are two encodings that never start an instruction anywhere in the function map: E034 appears only as the low word of pea.l operands (capstone also misdecodes it - roxr.l #8 for what silicon runs as roxr.b d0,d4 - but no rox instruction exists at any boundary in the map, so no rule is wrong on a path that exists), and 0072 00F6 01A0 01A0 sits inside data at 0x276c. The harness executes every distinct encoding it finds, code or not; silicon obliged, the port's rules for junk stay unverified, and that is the right place to leave them.
_names: Readability, ratcheted. addressNamed is how many routines are still called fn_<address>, which says where a routine came from and nothing about what it does; namedParams is how many parameters are more than the register they arrived in. The bar in DELIVERY.md is addressNamed 0, with every name backed by recorded evidence rather than being merely plausible - a wrong name is worse than an address, and 0x9080 was confidently called creditCompare while it drains an unrelated ring buffer. Move these numbers whenever a session names something: the edit is the record that the work happened. romlab/distinguish.py prints, per routine, the evidence needed to name it. The thing it showed: a colliding name is a name for a region (touches the player structs), and what separates its members is one level finer - the d(An) displacement, i.e. which field. No player routine reaches the struct by absolute address, so the field offsets are the whole distinguishing fact. Name the structs first and the routines name themselves; the other way round recovers the same field map forty-two times. 2026-08-01: the jump-stub rule now runs INSIDE the wrapper fixed point instead of once before it. It had a silent hole - the wrapper loop skips every `hop` address, so a stub whose target only became nameable later (because the target was itself a wrapper) could never be revisited, and stayed an address for ever. The two rules feed each other: a stub named this round is a callee for next round's wrapper, and a wrapper named this round is a target for next round's stub. Running both to a joint fixed point gives 48 wrappers and 31 of 67 stubs, and moves addressNamed from 539 to 537. A small number for the change, and worth saying why: most of those names already existed from the single pass, and what the fixed point adds is only the ones that were previously unreachable. The value is that the rule no longer depends on the order the two passes happen to run in, which is the kind of thing that silently stops working when something else moves. AND WHY THERE IS NO RULE LEFT FOR THE REMAINING 536, measured rather than assumed, so nobody spends a session looking for one. Of the unnamed routines, 415 have NO CALLERS AT ALL - they are inner entries reached by jump tables, tail jumps and lea(pc) continuations - so every caller-based rule is out for 77% of them: only 35 have exactly one caller that is itself named, and 44 have one to three all named. Proximity does not substitute: 536 of 537 have some named routine starting below them, but the median distance is 302 bytes and the commonest 'host' is a tiny wrapper with 86 entries after it, so naming by nearest-start-below would manufacture exactly the plausible-but-unchecked names this file exists to prevent. And of the 163 that genuinely sit INSIDE another routine's extent, the enclosing routine is unnamed in every single case - so the hosts have to be named first and the inner entries follow, not the other way round. That is the shape of the remaining work: it is evidence, one routine at a time, and DELIVERY.md was right to call it a bigger, less bounded grind. The two rules that DID generalise - wrappers named after their one callee, stubs named after where they jump - are now run to a joint fixed point and have given what they have to give. A NAMING FAULT FOUND WHILE TRACING, 2026-08-01, and it is the kind this file says is worse than an address. fn_07dce takes its d4 as `player_`, a role-inferred name - and at line 119 of its body assigns `player = (0x3e1968) >>> 0` and at line 143 uses it as `ptr`. The register is reused as a pointer for most of the routine, so the name is right for the first fifty lines and misleading for the rest. A scan for the same shape - a role-named parameter later reassigned to a constant address in work RAM - finds 331 of them. That is 331 of 2,852 named parameters - about one in eight - and the sentence that first stood here called it 'not a lot', which was written before the count came back and is simply wrong. It is a real defect rather than a missing name, and this file's own standard is that a wrong name costs more than fn_XXXXX does. Two ways to fix it and the second is better: refuse to name a parameter whose register is reassigned to an unrelated constant, or name it for what it holds on entry and let the reassignment introduce a new local, which is what a decompiler ought to do anyway since the two values have nothing to do with each other. roles.py assigns these names. The examples are not obscure ones either: kickWatchdogWrapper, helperInitialisePlayerStructs, wipeBoardRegionStartLevel (twice, in two different parameters), currentPieceDraw, cursorMove, counterReset and counterStep all take a parameter whose register is later pointed somewhere else entirely. So `namedParams` at 2,852 is an overcount of how much naming is actually TRUSTWORTHY: one in eight of those names is right on entry and wrong by the end of the routine. Worth fixing before the count is used as evidence of readability, because the readability bar in DELIVERY.md is about source somebody would choose to edit, and a parameter called `player` that holds a pointer halfway down is worse for an editor than one called d4. AND THE FIX IS IN, AT A COST THAT SHOULD BE STATED PLAINLY. roles.py now refuses to give a role name to a register that the routine later points at a constant address, because such a register is not one thing for the length of the routine and a role name claims it is. Result: routines with a parameter that stops being what it is called went from 331 to ZERO - and namedParams fell from 2852 to 2314, a loss of 538. That is a worse ratio than the 331 suggests, because the check is broader than the measurement was: it drops any register reassigned to a constant, not only ones reassigned into work RAM, and the extra couple of hundred are the same defect at other addresses. THE TRADE, argued rather than assumed: this file's standard is that a wrong name costs more than fn_XXXXX, and DELIVERY.md's bar is source somebody would choose to edit. A parameter called `player` that holds a pointer halfway down actively misleads the person editing, where `d4` merely tells them nothing. So fewer names that are true beats more names that are true for part of a routine. THE FLOOR IS LOWERED DELIBERATELY, from 2852 to 2314, which is the one thing a ratchet is not supposed to allow - recorded here so it is a decision on the record rather than a number that quietly slipped. The better fix, not done: name the parameter for what it holds on ENTRY and let the reassignment introduce a fresh local, since the two values have nothing to do with each other. That recovers the names honestly and is what a decompiler ought to do anyway. PARAMETERS, 2026-08-02: romlab/paramnames.py names a parameter after the callee it is handed to. A lifted call spills its arguments into the machine - setReg('d1', d1) - immediately before callRom, and the callee table says which of its parameters comes from d1 and what that parameter is called, so a local that is only ever passed on takes the name of what it is passed to. That is the same argument idents.py makes for naming a wrapper after the routine it wraps, and it compounds the same way, so it runs to a fixed point: 608 parameters over six rounds, 2304 to 2912. It is a rename and nothing else, which compose, writes and draws confirm - all three still report identity afterwards. The limit is the seed: only 675 of 1183 routines have a named register parameter to donate, so widening roles.py widens this too. THE RATCHET WAS LOWERED ON PURPOSE, 2026-08-02, from 3,069 to 3,036, and this is the record. Two changes to roles.py, in opposite directions. The first widened the comparison detector: the lifted form of a compare is not `x < y` - a `cmp` becomes setFlagsCmp and the branch a condition several layers of masking deep - so the adjacent-operator pattern matched 15 parameters in the whole file where a wider one matches 149. That added about 214 names. The second took more away: `limit` and `end` both mean 'a value this routine only ever tests against', and neither had ever checked that the parameter is not REASSIGNED. negateStore's d3 was called `limit` while the routine overwrites its low byte and then asks `>= 0` about the result - a working value, not a bound. About 247 names of that shape are gone. The guard was then corrected once more: the test is ORDER, not reassignment. Only two parameters in the whole file are overwritten before ever being read, so these registers really are inputs and are merely reused as scratch afterwards - a name for the test the routine performs is honest as long as the test happens before the reuse. Final: 3,137, up from 3,069, with roughly 247 misleading limit/end names removed and better ones put in their place. Do not 'fix' a future dip by loosening the guard; a wrong name is worse than the register it arrived in.
_decompKnownWrong: Routines whose lift disagrees with the oracle, by address. One left of 1,161: 0xB032 writes 0x1B where the machine writes 0x05 at 0x3E0A69, on every trial. Anything not named here fails the harness. WHAT IT IS, as of 2026-08-01: not an arithmetic difference but a CONTROL-FLOW one. 0xB032 has two call sites into 0xB5B8, `pea $5` at 0x0B0A2 and `pea $1b` at 0x0B1E0, and the constant that reaches 0x3E0A69 says which path ran. The branch is `tst.w -$8(a6)` at 0x0B1C8: the counter is zero on the chip and non-zero in the lift, so the lift enters the 0x1B block. Watched live - writes.test on 0x3E3228-0x3E3240 from interrupt 1490 - the decompiled run is plainly inside that block, pushing 1d1b, 1c1b, 1b1b, 1a1b, 191b, 181b through cellWriteHelper with an extra 0xB228 frame on its ROM stack, while the recompiled run never enters it. The counter is incremented in only two places, 0x0B108 and 0x0B1B0, each guarded by `bsr $b330` returning non-zero - and in decomp.test that callee runs on the ORACLE, so the fault is in how 0xB032 builds the argument it passes, not in 0xB330. RULED OUT: `lea $12(a7),a7` (handled, drops 18 and adjusts `pushed`); `move sr,d7`/`move d7,ccr` around 0x0B1BE, which used to bail and now lifts, with the restored CCR answering the branch - correct in itself, and it did NOT change this. Step-state cannot help: stepstate.log has no entry for 0xB032, so one.test.ts has nothing to compare against. THIS IS PROBABLY ALSO THE FIRST COMPOSED DIVERGENCE - the frame-1775 parting traces through fn_0b40a, which 0xB032 calls at 0x0B25A - so one fault likely closes both.
_stepstate: Routines whose state the port reproduces at the address the frozen chip stopped on. It was 0 - a zero floor, which hid a regression that took this harness from 832 to 95 when its entry list was regenerated out from under its captures. The floor is the measurement now.
_frames: How many exception frames the two dispatchers stack identically before the first that differs, from polls.test 'stack the same exception frame at every interrupt'. This replaces the old `writes` floor, which counted agreeing writes and was read as identity four separate times because the number it reported was the recording cap rather than the run. There is no writes floor now: the write comparison streams every write of every pattern to its own full length - 62 million across the six - and asserts identity, and compose asserts identity over work RAM, the playfield and the palette at every frame of every full game. What is left is this one number. Measured 2026-08-02: 1,219 of 2,125 interrupts on attract stack the same address and the same status register, and interrupt 1,220 at 0x444 differs in the X bit alone, 0x2314 against 0x2304. X outlives the instruction after it, so it can be set several routines back, and the lifted world writes its flags to the machine only at sync points - but SPILL_ALL=1, which spills at every block head, does not change the number, so a missing sync point is not the cause and the two sides genuinely disagree about the bit. The oracle last changed X at 0x3B76, `addq.w #$1,-$a(a6)`, whose lift emits the matching setXAdd inline; the disagreement is between there and 0x444 and is not located. It reaches memory only inside an exception frame, which the handler pops, which is why every other instrument reports identity. FOUR FAULTS WERE FIXED TO GET HERE, all of the same shape - something the recompiler did that the lift did not, or the reverse. (1) tick charged an interrupted block's cycles BEFORE running the handler, where the chip has not spent them yet, so the lifted side entered every handler ahead by that block's cost. (2) `move to sr` let an interrupt in without spilling the routine's registers, so the handler's movem saved stale values to the stack - the third place that needed the spill the block head already had. (3) THE ORACLE stacked the fall-through address after a taken branch instead of the target, because it read m.next, which the generated case sets to the fall-through before choosing the target; nothing noticed because rte pops the address and discards it. (4) xstate, the X bit's tracked state, was the one piece of carried state that did not reach a block from its predecessors, so a block inherited the X of whatever sat before it in ADDRESS order - and shifts never synced their condition codes at all, because sync_flags returned early for any kind that was not cmp, sub or add.

_screens: What is actually on the screen, which is a different question from whether memory matched and had to be asked separately. compose MODIFIED now renders the visible 336x240 picture out of each run's final snapshot - playfield byte through the palette - reports the differing pixels' bounding box, and writes both crops as PNG so they can be looked at. Two faults in the instrument had to go first: it digested the raw playfield rather than the picture, and `shot` was only populated during replay, so the first version compared two blank screens and reported 'no difference' for everything. Measured 2026-07-31 at 900 frames. attract and the long idle run differ only inside the wall glyphs at x 36..262, y 16..78 - that is the deliberate wallCellSet change and nothing else. The three-station and service-switch patterns lay no wall, so there is nothing to see. But `one player` and `two players` differ in 4608 pixels in a box at x 12..331, y 96..111, a full-width sixteen-pixel strip that is NOT wall: it is the station select banner, and the PNGs show both runs drawing the same words BLUE RED ORANGE with different panel colours - the recompiled run colours each panel to match its word, the decompiled run paints all three green. Reverting the hand edit reproduces the same 4608 pixels in the same box, so this is entirely independent of wallCellSet, and draws.test never saw it because draws.test only runs attract. Traced 2026-07-31 with writes.test: palette writes are identical (7090 of them, W_LO=0x3c0000 W_HI=0x3c1000), so it is not the palette - it is the playfield bytes. Windowed on the strip itself (W_LO=0x20c000 W_HI=0x20e000) the two part at write 26216 of 31528, at 0x20c00c, recompiled 0x9b against decompiled 0x8b: one bit, 0x10, and the high nibble of a colour index is the palette bank. The stack names graphicsDecompressor under decompressOneEightPixelColumnFrom1, and the lift shows the stored byte is (d3.w >>> 4) + d2.w where d2 is the colour base the caller passes in as arg8. graphicsDecompressor is not in decompKnownWrong - it verifies clean against the oracle on random states - so the suspect is upstream: a caller selecting a different palette bank for the banner panels. That is the next thing to chase and it is the first genuinely wrong thing found on screen rather than in memory. TRACED FURTHER 2026-07-31 with the new ROM-stack walk. The caller is fn_036a2, which pushes d1 as the decompressor's arg8, and builds it as d1 = (load8(ptr) << 4) + load16(dst - 2). The stack shows that product as 0x90 against 0x80, so load8(ptr) is 9 in the recompiled run and 8 in the decompiled one - and ptr itself differs, 0x3f179 against 0x3ef80. The two runs are reading the colour out of different records, so this is not a lifting fault in the drawing path at all: it is downstream of a work-RAM state difference, and work RAM does diverge on this pattern at write 582,338 (see _writes). The banner is the first place that difference becomes visible, which makes it the symptom and the counters at 0x3e327x the disease. NARROWED 2026-08-01, and it is not what the seam would predict. The ROM stack walker reports IDENTICAL call chains at the differing write - 0x11f1e <- 0xeb0 <- 0x3708 <- 0x10000 <- 0x7df8 <- 0x10000 <- 0x92d4 <- ... <- 0x91fc in both runs - with the same a6 and the same frame. So neither run took a different path; the same code ran with the same callers and produced a different colour. And it is not an animation phase: rendered at 870 frames as well as 900, the recompiled banner is blue/red/orange both times and the decompiled is green both times, so the fault is stable rather than a one-frame offset in something that cycles. That rules out the explanation the timing seam would give and leaves a data difference: the colour base the caller pushes as arg8, which graphicsDecompressor adds as d2 and which differs by exactly 0x10, the palette bank. NEXT: log arg8 at entry to decompressOneEightPixelColumnFrom1 in both runs and diff the first call where they part, then walk back to where that value is read. The caller chain above gives the exact routines to look in, and 0x3708 is the one that pushes six longs and tail-jumps into the tileset entry. CONFIRMED AT THE ARGUMENT, 2026-08-01. writes.test now records d2 per write alongside a6, and at the divergence it reads 0x200090 against 0x200080 - the colour base differs by exactly 0x10, which is the whole fault one level above the pixel. graphicsDecompressor is therefore innocent: it stores (d3.w >>> 4) + d2.w and is faithfully drawing the bank it was handed. The value carries a playfield address in its upper half (0x200000) with the colour in the low byte, so whatever computes it is deriving both together. Combined with the identical ROM stacks and the stability across frames, the fault is now localised to: one routine in the chain 0xeb0 / 0x3708 / 0x7df8 / 0x92d4 computing a low byte of 0x90 where the oracle computes 0x80. NEXT: window writes.test on wherever that value is stored before the push, or read the lift of 0x3708 and 0xeb0 for a bit-4 operation on a byte - the arithmetic is small enough that a wrong flag or a dropped bit will be visible on inspection. This is the first fault this session that is a plain lifting bug rather than a question about the seam, and it is the one worth finishing. CORRECTION, same day, before the previous paragraph misleads anyone: the banner is probably NOT an independent lifting bug. The routine at 0x33f4 that calls into the tileset entry pushes d2 through unchanged - it is a pass-through, and the value arrives from further up. And every routine in the chain passes decomp.test against the oracle on random machine states; the only routine known to fail is 0xB032, which is not in this chain. A rule bug would fail there. So the wrong colour base is state-dependent, which makes it most likely DOWNSTREAM of the work-RAM divergence at write 23,999 rather than a separate fault - the same root reaching the screen. That also explains what looked contradictory: stable across frames because the state went wrong once and stayed wrong, not because something is mis-lifted on every call. THE TEST THAT SETTLES IT: find the earliest frame at which the banner is drawn at all, and compare it against the frame of the first work-RAM divergence. Banner wrong BEFORE any divergence means independent; wrong only after means downstream, and then there is one bug here rather than two. Do that before spending time reading 0xeb0 and 0x7df8 - the previous paragraph sends you there, and it may be sending you after a symptom. AND THE TEST WAS RUN. At 340 frames the two runs' screens are identical - nothing to see. At 400 frames the only difference is 255 pixels in a box at x 52..262, y 16..31, which is the wall-glyph footprint of the deliberate wallCellSet change and nothing else. The banner box at y 96..111 appears only in the longer runs. So the banner difference emerges somewhere after frame 400, well past the first divergence at frame 351, which supports the correction above: it is downstream, not independent. The caveat that keeps this short of proof is that the banner may not be drawn at all at frame 400 - a difference cannot appear in something that is not yet on screen - and establishing the frame at which the station-select banner is first drawn would settle it outright. The cheap way is to render the y 96..111 strip from a single run at increasing frame counts and find where it stops being blank. Worth doing before anyone treats the banner as a second bug: on the evidence so far there is one root divergence, and the green banner is what it looks like by the time it reaches the screen. SWEPT BY FRAME COUNT, and the answer is more interesting than either guess. 340: screens identical. 400: 255 pixels, the wall glyphs. 500: 380 pixels, the wall glyphs. 600: IDENTICAL AGAIN - nothing at all. 700: 4608 pixels, the banner strip at y 96..111. So the screens RECONVERGE: whatever the wall difference was, it leaves the screen entirely by frame 600, the two runs agree completely, and only then does the banner appear and appear wrong. That means the banner is wrong the FIRST time it is drawn rather than drifting into wrongness, which weakens the downstream reading recorded above - a screen that agrees at 600 is not a screen carrying visible accumulated error into 700. It does not restore the independent reading either, because memory can differ while the screen agrees, and work RAM is known to part at write 23,999. What it does establish is the shape of the thing: a single drawing operation, on its first execution, using a colour base 0x10 too high. That is a much smaller target than 'state diverged somewhere'. The reconvergence at 600 is also a fact worth keeping on its own - it is the first evidence in this project that the two runs can differ visibly and then agree again, which means visible divergence is not necessarily permanent and a screen comparison at a single frame count can miss and find the same fault depending where it lands. AND THE DIRECTION IS KNOWN. The oracle holds 0x200090 and the lift holds 0x200080: bit 4 is CLEAR in the decompiled value where the recompiled sets it. So this is a dropped bit rather than a wrong computation, and the oracle says which way. That is the same family as the bclr/bset fault fixed earlier this session and recorded in _writes - that one dropped the FLAGS a bit instruction sets, this one would drop the VALUE - which is worth noting because the earlier fix was found by diffing decomp.py against m68kts.py and finding a rule the recompiler had and the lifter did not. That is the first thing to try here: grep both emitters for the instructions that set a single bit in a register (bset, or.b with a power of two, and the addq/andi forms) and compare them rule by rule. If the rule is present and correct in both, the next suspect is the value's PROVENANCE rather than its arithmetic - something reads it from memory that was written correctly and re-reads it after something else cleared it. Either way the search is now bounded to single-bit operations on one value, which is as small as this has been. EXPERIMENT RUN, AND IT IS DECISIVE. POKE=1 forces the four bytes at 0x3E3274 to zero in BOTH runs from the frame callback, which fires just before the handler that reads them. With it on, the two runs' visible screens are IDENTICAL at 700 frames and at 900 - the 4,608-pixel banner difference disappears completely. The control rules out the poke simply breaking the game: at 500 frames it still reports 380 pixels in the wall-glyph box at x 36..262, y 16..78, which is the deliberate wallCellSet change, so the game is running and drawing normally and only the residue was neutralised. THE CONCLUSION: the green station banner is caused entirely by the stack residue at 0x3E3274, which differs because the two dispatchers push exception frames at different instants. It is not a lifting fault, no routine is mis-translated, and nothing in the port computes a wrong colour - the game reads a word of stack nobody wrote and draws a palette bank out of it. That closes a question this file has carried since the screens were first compared, and it means the visible divergence and the write divergence are one phenomenon with one cause. WHAT IT LEAVES: the residue is real and the game does depend on it, so 'the same picture on every pattern' is reachable only by making the exception frames agree or by excluding reads of uninitialised stack the way interruptFrame is already excluded. That is a decision about what the comparison means, not a bug to fix, and it should be made deliberately rather than by widening a mask until the red goes away.
_romstack: How to find the caller, which the JavaScript stack cannot tell you. Both dispatchers are trampolines - a routine calls another by returning to the loop with a new program counter - so ROM call depth is not JS call depth and writes.test's `stack:` line bottoms out in `call <- callDecompiled <- callRom` no matter how deep the ROM is. The chain is on the machine's own stack and in the same form in both runs, so writes.test now walks it at the divergence and prints both. It reads longwords at every two bytes, so consecutive entries overlap and half of what it prints is a shifted duplicate of its neighbour - read every other one, and check any address against facts.json before believing it. It paid for itself immediately: on the banner-colour fault it showed 0x11f1e (the return into the decompressor wrapper), then the pushed arguments, of which one read 0x90 in the recompiled run and 0x80 in the decompiled - the colour bank, the whole bug, sitting in plain sight on the stack.
_3e32xx: What the 0x3E3200-0x3E32C0 window actually is, because the name it was given was wrong. Windowed there on `one player` (2026-07-31) the runs part at write 23,967 of 252,189, and the writes descend - 0x3e3280, then 0x3e327e, then 0x3e327c - with a7 sitting at 0x3e327e and a6 at 0x3e32c2. That is the machine stack, not a sound sequencer's state: these are pushes, and what differs is the contents of registers being spilled. The ROM stack walk prints the same chain for both runs, longword for longword, so the call path is identical and only the values are apart: 0x504e against 0x4fb3 at 0x3e3280, and 0x1d18 against 0x1d10 at 0x3e3274, under counterStep into extractsOwnerBitsCellByte. Same shape as the known seam at fn_00430 - a register spill exposing a value the two dispatchers hold differently - but here it is NOT self-evidently the seam, because it propagates: this is the same divergence that, further on, hands fn_036a2 a different record pointer and paints the station banner green (see _screens). So the open question is precisely whether 0x504e/0x4fb3 is interrupt-timing residue or a real counter, and that is what to answer next. First discriminator run 2026-07-31: WAIT_SKIP=1 leaves the divergence at exactly write 23,967, unmoved. So this is NOT the fn_00430 spin loop that accounts for the frame-351 seam - excluding that loop entirely changes nothing here. Taken with the identical ROM stacks, that means the two runs walk the same code path with the same call chain and hold different values in registers, for a reason not yet identified and not the known seam. Worth noting but not yet meaningful: 0x504e - 0x4fb3 is 0x9B, 155, and the cycle clocks are 142 apart at the first write in this window, which is the right order of magnitude for a cycle-derived quantity - but the game cannot read a cycle counter, so if that resemblance is real it has to arrive through something paced by interrupts. SETTLED 2026-07-31, and it changes the answer to the whole equivalence question. IRQ_PHASE shifts the first interrupt; run the same window at phase 0 and phase 1511 and both dispatchers return byte-identical values - recompiled 0x504e at both, decompiled 0x4fb3 at both. Residue of where an interrupt landed moves when the phase moves. This does not. So 0x504e is a quantity the game computed and 0x4fb3 is the decompilation computing it wrongly: a REAL lifting fault, not a seam, and therefore fixable. That matters beyond this one value, because the standing assumption - that what is left between the two runs is the interrupt seam - is now known to be false for at least this divergence, and byte-identity through a full game is back on the table rather than argued away.
